examples.en: I saw a turtle at the zoo.
A turtle walks slowly.
Tortoises are animals that live a long time.
The child slept hugging a toy turtle.
The tortoise and the hare had a race.
I fed the turtle at the beach.

explain: '거북이'라는 말도 같이 써요. 아주 느린 걸음을 비유할 때는 '거북이걸음'이라고 해요.
explain_en: The form 'geobugi' is also used. A very slow pace is described figuratively as 'geobugigeoreum' (turtle walk).

examples.en: The child blew up a balloon and it popped.
The balloon floated away into the sky.

examples.ko: 생일 파티에 고무풍선을 열 개 달았어요.
examples.en: I hung ten balloons at the birthday party.
A rubber balloon pops when it touches a needle.
I wrote a name on a balloon and gave it as a gift.
Please buy me just one balloon.

explain: 그냥 '풍선'이라고 해도 보통 같은 물건을 말해요. 불다, 터지다, 날아가다 같은 말과 같이 많이 써요.
explain_en: Just saying '풍선' usually refers to the same thing. It goes with verbs like 불다 (blow up), 터지다 (pop) and 날아가다 (fly away).

examples.en: On the weekend I went to the public bathhouse with my father.
At a public bathhouse, you shower and then get into the tub.
Public bathhouses have decreased a lot these days.

examples.ko: 어릴 때 공중목욕탕에서 먹던 바나나우유가 생각나요.
examples.en: I remember the banana milk I drank at the bathhouse as a kid.

examples.ko: 공중목욕탕 가는 날은 온 가족이 일찍 일어났어요.
examples.en: On bathhouse days, the whole family woke up early.

examples.ko: 이 동네에는 오래된 공중목욕탕이 하나 있어요.
examples.en: There is one old public bathhouse in this neighborhood.

explain: 일상에서는 그냥 '목욕탕'이라고 많이 말해요. 여러 사람이 함께 쓰는 곳이라 공중도덕을 지켜야 해요.
explain_en: In daily speech people often just say '목욕탕'. Many people share the space, so you need to follow public etiquette.

examples.en: The baby kicks every time I change the diaper.
Someone kept kicking in their sleep, so I slept poorly.
I kicked hard at the ball, but missed.

examples.ko: 아기가 좋아서 다리를 흔들며 발길질하고 있어요.
examples.en: The baby is happily waving and kicking its legs.
Please don't kick around on the bed.

examples.ko: 발길질하면 다칠 수 있으니까 장난으로도 하지 마세요.
examples.en: Kicking can hurt someone, so don't do it even as a joke.

explain: '발로 차다'와 달리 발을 계속 휘두르거나 여러 번 차는 느낌이 있어요. '발길질을 하다'로도 말해요. 수영에서 발을 움직이는 동작은 보통 '발차기'라고 해요.
explain_en: Unlike '발로 차다', it gives a feeling of swinging the feet around or kicking repeatedly. You can also say '발길질을 하다'. In swimming, the leg motion is usually called '발차기'.

examples.en: I rode a boat on the lake on the weekend.
A small boat slowly crosses the river.
We ate lunch on the boat.
I'd like to rent a boat.
The wind is blowing, so the boat rocks a lot.
Kids love rubber boats.

explain: '배'는 크든 작든 물에 뜨는 탈것 전체를 부르고, '보트'는 놀이나 구조에 쓰는 작은 배에 써요. 큰 배는 '선박'이나 '유람선'이라고 해요. '보트를 타다', '보트를 젓다'처럼 써요.
explain_en: '배' is the general word for any floating vessel, big or small, while '보트' is a small boat for fun or rescue. Large ships are called '선박' or '유람선'. It goes with verbs like '보트를 타다' (ride a boat) and '보트를 젓다' (row a boat).

examples.en: I'm not unhappy right now.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 불행한 일을 많이 겪었어요.
examples.en: That person went through many unfortunate events.
He had an unhappy-looking face.
You can be unhappy even if you have a lot of money.
Unfortunately, it rained and the event was canceled.
She said her childhood was unhappy.

explain: 반대말은 '행복하다'예요. '불행하다'는 꽤 무거운 말이라서 오늘 기분이 안 좋을 때는 '속상해요', '우울해요'를 더 많이 써요. '불행하게도'는 나쁜 소식을 전할 때 앞에 붙이는 말이에요.
explain_en: The opposite is 행복하다. 불행하다 is a fairly heavy word, so for a bad mood today you would say 속상해요 or 우울해요 instead. 불행하게도 is placed in front when you deliver bad news.

examples.en: I got a zero on the test and was upset.
If you don't write your name, it's graded as zero.

examples.ko: 빵점 맞은 시험지를 친구가 보여 줬어요.
examples.en: My friend showed me the test paper he got zero on.
I didn't expect to get a zero.
I didn't get a single question right, so it's a zero.

examples.ko: 빵점 받을까 봐 걱정했는데 다행히 아니었어요.
examples.en: I was worried about getting a zero, but luckily I didn't.

explain: '영점'보다 '빵점'이 일상 대화에서 훨씬 편하게 쓰는 말이에요. 반의어는 '만점'이고, '빵점을 받다/맞다'라고 해요.

phrases.nuance_ko: 점수와 상관없이 어떤 것이 아주 형편없다고 평가할 때 써요. 주로 '태도가 빵점', '센스가 빵점'처럼 말해요.
phrases.nuance_en: It is used to say something is very poor even when no score is involved, as in '태도가 빵점' or '센스가 빵점'.

explain_en: '빵점' is the casual everyday word, much more relaxed than '영점'. The opposite is '만점' (full marks), and you say '빵점을 받다' or '빵점을 맞다'.

examples.ko: 헌 가방 말고 새것을 사고 싶어요.
examples.en: I want to buy a new one, not an old bag.
These shoes are clean, like new.
A new one is expensive, so I bought a used one.
I threw away the worn cup and replaced it with a new one.
If you need a new one, go to the shop and ask.

examples.ko: 이 책은 아직 새것이라서 아껴서 읽어요.
examples.en: This book is still new, so I read it carefully.

explain: '새 옷', '새 가방'처럼 물건 이름을 같이 말하면 '새'를 써요. 이미 말한 물건을 다시 가리킬 때는 '새것'이라고 해요. 반대는 '헌것'이나 '낡은 것'이에요.
explain_en: When you name the item, you use '새' as in '새 옷' and '새 가방'. When you point back to an item you already mentioned, you say 새것. The opposite is '헌것' or '낡은 것'.

examples.en: A light drizzle has been falling since this morning.
It was only a drizzle, so I just walked without an umbrella.

examples.ko: 이슬비는 소리 없이 내려서 잘 몰라요.
examples.en: A drizzle falls without a sound, so you hardly notice it.
My clothes got a little wet in the drizzle.
I drank tea watching the drizzle outside the window.
On drizzly days I think of pajeon.

explain: 아주 가늘게 내리는 비예요. '가랑비', '보슬비', '안개비'도 가는 비를 가리키는 말이에요. 일기예보에서는 '약한 비'라고 하는 경우가 많아요.
explain_en: It is very fine, light rain. '가랑비', '보슬비' and '안개비' also refer to light rain. Weather forecasts often just say '약한 비' (light rain).

examples.en: We ate lunch boxes on the park lawn.
After even mowing the yard lawn, I am tired.
Lawn grass grows fast in summer.
You must not walk on the grass.
It rained, so the grass grew green.
They laid new turf on the soccer field.

explain: 잔디는 '잔디를 깎다', '잔디를 심다'처럼 써요. 길가에 저절로 나는 '풀'과 달리 곱게 가꾸는 풀이에요. 잔디가 깔린 넓은 곳은 '잔디밭'이라고 해요.
explain_en: 잔디 is used as in '잔디를 깎다' (mow the lawn) and '잔디를 심다' (plant grass). Unlike '풀' that grows by itself along the road, it is grass that is tended. A wide area covered with it is a '잔디밭'.

examples.ko: 그 물건은 몇몇 재래시장에서만 구할 수 있어요.
examples.en: You can only find that item at a few traditional markets.

examples.ko: 어머니는 생필품을 살 때 재래시장보다 슈퍼를 더 자주 이용하세요.
examples.en: When buying daily necessities, my mother uses supermarkets more than traditional markets.
On the weekend I bought fresh vegetables at the traditional market.

examples.ko: 재래시장은 값을 깎을 수 있어서 좋아요.
examples.en: I like traditional markets because you can bargain.
The traditional market in our neighborhood got renovated.
I went to see a traditional market with a foreign friend.

explain: 마트에서는 값이 정해져 있지만 재래시장에서는 깎아 달라고 말하기도 해요. '전통시장'도 거의 같은 뜻으로 써요. 마트·백화점과 짝으로 비교해서 말할 때가 많아요.
explain_en: Prices are fixed at marts, but at a traditional market people sometimes ask for a discount. '전통시장' is used with almost the same meaning. It is often contrasted with marts and department stores.

examples.en: The game was stopped because of the rain.
We're suspending the construction for a while this week.
Even though it's hard, I don't want to stop my diet.

examples.ko: 처방받은 약은 마음대로 중단하면 안 돼요.
examples.en: You must not stop taking prescribed medicine on your own.

examples.ko: 그 회사는 다음 달에 서비스를 중단할 예정이에요.
examples.en: That company plans to discontinue the service next month.
Please explain why you stopped so suddenly.

explain: '그만두다'는 학교·일·습관을 끊을 때 일상에서 쓰고, '중단하다'는 공사·방송·서비스처럼 공식적인 상황에 많이 써요. 차나 시계처럼 움직임이 서는 건 '멈추다'예요. 멈췄던 걸 다시 시작하면 '재개하다'라고 해요.
explain_en: '그만두다' is the everyday word for quitting school, a job or a habit, while 중단하다 is used more for construction, broadcasts and services in formal situations. When movement stops, as with a car or a clock, use '멈추다'. Starting again after a stop is '재개하다'.

examples.en: The bathroom tile is cracked and water leaks.
Tiles are fairly resistant to water.

examples.ko: 집주인이 주방 벽에 타일을 새로 붙였어요.
examples.en: The landlord put new tiles on the kitchen wall.
Water splashed on the tile, so I wiped it.
We decorated the wall with white tiles.
Tiles also come in a wide variety of colors and shapes.

explain: 욕실이나 주방의 벽과 바닥에 붙이는 얇은 판이에요. '욕실 타일', '벽 타일'처럼 장소 이름과 함께 써요. 물에 강해서 물을 많이 쓰는 곳에 붙여요.
explain_en: It is a thin plate set on bathroom and kitchen walls and floors, so it combines with place names like '욕실 타일' and '벽 타일'. It resists water, so it goes in places that get wet a lot.

examples.en: I can see children picking grapes in the vineyard.
Grandfather runs a small vineyard.
The vineyard stretched out endlessly.
In autumn we go on a field trip to the vineyard.
There is a small road beside the vineyard.
This village's vineyards are very famous.

explain: 작물 이름 뒤에 '밭'을 붙여 '배추밭', '고구마밭', '포도밭'처럼 말해요. 쌀을 기르는 곳은 '밭'이 아니라 '논'이에요. 과일나무를 키우는 곳은 '과수원'이라고도 해요.
explain_en: You add 밭 after the crop name, as in 배추밭, 고구마밭 and 포도밭. The place where rice grows is not a 밭 but a 논. A place that grows fruit trees can also be called a 과수원.

examples.ko: 밥을 먹고 나서 행주로 식탁을 닦아요.
examples.en: After eating, I wipe the table with a dishcloth.
Every weekend I wash the dishcloth clean and hang it up.
Excuse me, could you give me a dishcloth here?
I dry a wet dishcloth in the sun on the balcony.
I took a new dishcloth out of the drawer.

examples.ko: 행주에서 냄새가 나면 뜨거운 물에 삶아요.
examples.en: When the dishcloth smells, I boil it in hot water.

explain: 식탁이나 그릇을 닦는 깨끗한 천은 '행주', 바닥을 닦는 천은 '걸레'예요. 두 단어를 바꿔 쓰면 이상해요. 행주는 '빨다, 삶다, 짜다'와 함께 써요.
explain_en: The clean cloth for tables and dishes is 'haengju', and the cloth for floors is 'geolle'. Swapping them sounds odd. Haengju goes with verbs like '빨다' (wash), '삶다' (boil) and '짜다' (wring out).

en: cancel a class; cancellation of a class

examples.en: The professor is sick, so today's class is canceled.

examples.ko: 학교 홈페이지 공지를 보고서야 휴강인 걸 알았어요.
examples.en: I only found out the class was canceled after seeing the notice on the school website.

examples.ko: 비가 많이 와서 내일 수업이 휴강됐대요.
examples.en: I heard tomorrow's class is canceled because of heavy rain.

examples.ko: 이번 주 금요일에는 휴강한다고 교수님이 말씀하셨어요.
examples.en: The professor said there's no class this Friday.
When is the make-up class if the professor cancels?

examples.ko: 갑자기 휴강이라서 친구들과 영화를 보러 갔어요.
examples.en: Class was suddenly canceled, so I went to see a movie with friends.

explain: 교수님이 수업을 취소하는 쪽은 '휴강하다', 수업 쪽에서 말할 땐 '휴강이다', '휴강되다'라고 해요. 짝말은 '보강'으로, 쉬는 수업을 나중에 채우는 수업이에요.
explain_en: When the professor cancels, you say '휴강하다'; from the class's side you say '휴강이다' or '휴강되다'. Its partner word is '보강', a make-up class held later.

examples.ko: 이 요리는 힘들이지 않고도 금방 만들 수 있어요.
examples.en: You can make this dish quickly without much effort.

examples.ko: 친구가 힘들여서 구해 온 책이라 소중해요.
examples.en: My friend went to a lot of trouble to get this book, so it's precious to me.

examples.ko: 힘들인 만큼 좋은 결과가 나올 거예요.
examples.en: You'll get good results in proportion to the effort you put in.

examples.ko: 힘들일 필요 없이 그냥 버튼만 누르세요.
examples.en: No need to strain yourself, just press the button.

examples.ko: 처음부터 너무 힘들이면 오래 못 해요.
examples.en: If you push too hard from the start, you can't keep going for long.

examples.ko: 어제는 별로 힘들이지 않았는데 결과가 아주 좋았어요.
examples.en: I didn't put in much effort yesterday, but the result was very good.

explain: '힘들다'(어렵다)와 달리 힘을 들인다는 뜻의 동사라서 목적어와 함께 써요. '힘들이지 않고', '힘들여서'처럼 쓰는 경우가 많고, '애쓰다'나 '공을 들이다'와 비슷해요.
explain_en: Unlike '힘들다' (hard), this is a verb meaning to put effort in, so it takes an object. It most often appears as '힘들이지 않고' or '힘들여서', and it is close to '애쓰다' and '공을 들이다'.
